lessonRef.subject: mathematics
lessonRef.focus: inference from a sample to a population
lessonRef.title: Transfer challenge: inference from a sample to a population

sections.title: Instructional examples
sections.directions: The example is from a different context than the problems below.

items.prompt: n = 400, sample proportion 55%. Margin and interval?

sections.title: Independent practice
sections.directions: Work on your own. Show the steps that produced each answer.

items.prompt: In 500 simulations under the assumption of no difference, 2 produced a result at least as extreme as the one observed. What should be concluded?
choices: The simulation proves that the observed difference is real.
The observed result is statistically significant: it occurred in only 0.4% of simulations, below the usual 5% threshold.
The observed result is not statistically significant: it occurred in 0.4% of simulations, which is not unusual.
The simulation proves that there is no difference.

items.prompt: A quantity is approximately normal with mean 150 and standard deviation 15. Approximately what percentage of values lie between 135 and 165?
choices: about 68%
about 50%
about 95%
about 99.7%

items.prompt: A researcher runs a randomised controlled experiment with participants randomly assigned to treatments. What kind of conclusion does this design support?
choices: It supports both generalisation and causation, provided the sample is large.
It supports a causal conclusion about the treatment, within the population studied.
It supports generalising from the sample to the population, but not a causal claim.
It supports neither generalisation nor causation, because self-selection can bias both.

items.prompt: A random sample of 2500 people gives a sample proportion of 73%. Using the conservative margin of error 1/√n, give the approximate margin of error and the resulting interval.
choices: ±4%, giving 69% to 77%
±2%, giving 71% to 75%
±73%, giving 0% to 146%
±0%, giving 73% to 73%

items.prompt: In 100 simulations under the assumption of no difference, 1 produced a result at least as extreme as the one observed. What should be concluded?
choices: The observed result is not statistically significant: it occurred in 1% of simulations, which is not unusual.
The observed result is statistically significant: it occurred in only 1% of simulations, below the usual 5% threshold.
The simulation proves that there is no difference.
The simulation proves that the observed difference is real.

sections.title: Extension and challenge
sections.directions: These are meant to be hard. Show the reasoning even if you do not finish.

items.prompt: A quantity is approximately normal with mean 195 and standard deviation 9. Approximately what percentage of values lie between 177 and 213?
items.responseExpectation: Give the result and the reasoning that produced it. Show enough work that someone else could check each step.

items.prompt: A researcher runs a sample survey with randomly selected participants. What kind of conclusion does this design support?
items.responseExpectation: Give the result and the reasoning that produced it. Show enough work that someone else could check each step.

items.prompt: A random sample of 400 people gives a sample proportion of 53%. Using the conservative margin of error 1/√n, give the approximate margin of error and the resulting interval.
items.responseExpectation: Give the result and the reasoning that produced it. Show enough work that someone else could check each step.
